title: Grouping Handlers by File Extension
body: Dispatching on suffix makes JSON and CSV loader flow clear. Use suffix.lower() if uppercase extensions are accepted, and handle each parser's exceptions because an extension does not validate content. Report the supported extensions for unknown input.

title: Reading and Writing JSON
body: You can read a string from a JSON file using `read_text()` and convert it to Python data using `json.loads()`. Conversely, when saving the result, you can convert Python data to a JSON string using `json.dumps()`.
detail: It’s easy to understand the JSON processing flow as a process that moves back and forth between strings and Python data. `input_path.read_text(encoding='utf-8')` reads the file contents as a string, and `json.loads(text)` converts that string into a dictionary or list. To save the processed results, use `json.dumps(data, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)` to create a human-readable JSON string, then save it using `write_text()`. If the data contains Korean characters, using `ensure_ascii=False` makes the output easier to read.

title: CSV DictReader and DictWriter
body: csv.DictReader allows you to read CSV rows as a dictionary organized by column names. csv.DictWriter is used to save a list of dictionaries back to CSV, and you use `fieldnames` to specify the column names and their order.
detail: If the first line of a CSV file is a header, beginners will find it easier to read the file using `DictReader`. This is because each row can be accessed by its column name, such as `row['name']`. When saving, use `DictWriter` and specify the column names in `fieldnames`. `writeheader()` writes the header row, and `writerows(rows)` saves multiple rows. It’s also a good idea to learn how to use `newline=''` and `encoding='utf-8'` together to handle CSV files safely.

title: Creating a Data Summary
body: File-processing CLIs often generate summary results—such as the number of rows, a list of columns, a list of keys, and the number of errors—rather than simply copying the original data. If you store the summary in a dictionary, it’s easy to use for both saving as JSON and displaying on the screen.
detail: For example, if you’ve read a CSV file, you can store the number of rows and a list of columns in a `summary` dictionary. If the JSON is a list, you can count the number of items; if it’s a dictionary, you can create a list of keys. A summary created this way is easy to save using `json.dumps()` and can be easily expanded into logs or reports later. The key point is to separate reading, processing, and saving—rather than mixing them all into a single line—by using a function like `make_summary()`.
